replies.author: @wkgurr
replies.text: Alicudi used to have 800 or more inhabitants at the time the terraces and footpaths where built. The moment emigration became an option almost everybody left and descendants of former Alicudaris today live in Australia or the US. The emigrants left behind the houses they used to live in. Over the years many of those houses fell into ruins until in the late 1960s and early 70s people from Northern Europe (mostly from Germany, Switzerland and Austria)  discovered the beauty of the islands and began buying the ruins, which they then had renovated. In those years you could buy a ruin for an apple and an egg (if you managed to sort out the complicated ownership issues) but these days are over. So most of the houses above a few 100 steps in elevation are empty most of the year and are only visited by their mostly absent owners for a few weeks every year. The true Alciudaris (i.e. the descendants of those who chose not to emigrate) have moved to houses close to the "harbor". To encounter the 100 inhabitants situation you'd have to visit between December and March. Outside of that time window there are always more than 100 people present on the island. However, due to the steepness of the terrain and the requirement for serious physical excertion to get anywhere you can find plenty of absolutely deserted corners on this island, even at the very height of the tourist season.

replies.author: @wkgurr
replies.text: This is not an option as dehumidifcation requires huge amounts of energy (use ai to do a few calculations yourself re "latent heat"). A large solar plant would have to be installed to cover the needs. And on Alicudi as everywhere on the Eolian Islands the aesthetic aspect is important. You do not want the entire flank of a mountain covered with solar panels. Furthermore, dehumdification only works during the hot and humid summer months, when dew points are well above 20 C. Alicudi already uses natural dehumidification by collecting rainwater. Sea water desalination is a more realistic option for fresh water production and it is currently under consideration.

replies.author: @wkgurr
replies.text: Alicudi has its own power station (this was the main reason for building the road along the coast, namely to get the diesel to the generators) and the electric grid covers almost the entire inhabited section of the island. So there is electric light, fridges and freezers, pumps etc. Each house has a soak pit or a dry toilet. Soak pits are used in many parts of the world where there is no sewage system (also in the US). Cooking is done with propane gas cylinders or electric hobs. Each house has one or more cisterns with rain water capture from the roof of the house. In addition, at lower elevations there is also piped water from a large cistern further up the hill which gets filled by a water ship that arrives once or twice a month, depending and the fresh water demands.

replies.author: @wkgurr
replies.text: @ImpossiblePlacesGlobal Installing a sea water desalination plant is currently under discussion and there was recently a meeting where the local population was informed about this project and could ask questions. There are many issues that need to be sorted out before a plant for desalination of sea water can be installed: Sea water intake, and brine outflow, energy needs (does the Alicudi power station need to be expanded to cover the additional requirements this plant would cause?). Who maintains and repairs it? How are prolonged failures bridged? All houses of Alicudi still have their cistern(s) and even today with the watership arriving regularly these act as buffer and additional storage space. So if the issues can be addressed comprehensively, a sea water desalination plant would be a nice thing to have and a good use of the grants that have been obtained from the Italian gvt and/or the EU.

replies.author: @ImpossiblePlacesGlobal
replies.text: @silverbuyer That is indeed a red Iveco truck right there. Let me explain the secret behind it:This is actually a very special exception on Alicudi. The flat concrete area right by the pier is the only place on the entire island where a vehicle can actually move. The truck is brought over by ferry from the mainland, and its only job is to hang around the port to help unload heavy goods and building materials from the big boats.But if you look closely at the photo, you can see a really cool transition: the truck can only go a few meters before it has to stop. Then, all the supplies are immediately transferred onto the backs of those donkeys waiting right next to it, so they can carry them up the steep stone steps! Once you go past the port, there are absolutely no roads for cars.So, Alicudi is still technically a completely car-free island, keeping its beautiful, untouched charm.

replies.author: @wkgurr
replies.text: The reason the road was built, was the erection of the Alicudi power station. It contains diesel-powered generators that deliver electricity to the local grid. The sea between the islands dips to more than 1200m in depth and the seabed is not suitable for the laying of electric cables. The generators need diesel to run and that fuel is delivered by trucks that need to drive from the ferry to the power station. There would be enough sun to allow for the Alicudaris to live off solar power, but at the time the power station was built, solar would have required a much larger investment. Today, many Alicudaris have individually installed solar power, which serves to reduce electricity costs and ties them over when the power station is down, which happens every now and then. Since the power station is maintained by technicians from Lipari or the mainland it may take several days for it to be repaired in situations where the weather does not allow for ship or helicopter traffic. Having a road along the sea is a big plus as it allows parking of vehicles belonging to residents living higher up. A parked vehicle can act as a storage space for goods that need to be transported uphill. Furthermore, the road has facilitated the task of rubbish collection as large containers full of rubbish can now be loaded onto the ferry. It is true that Alicudi  - apart from this road  - is entirely unsuited to any wheeled transport (including bicycles) as everthing is stairs and steps. Recently, on this road I could observe one of the local girls learning how to drive a car. A friend of hers must have brought his car from the mainland and she was sitting behind the wheele going back and forth on those 200 m while looking frightened and intensely focused.

replies.text: @esthergabriel5012 Here is exactly how it works: Alicudi is technically 'car-free' because there are zero public roads, streets, or personal cars for driving around. The island is just a steep volcanic cone made entirely of stone steps.However, there is one tiny exception: the small, flat concrete strip right at the port. A couple of utility trucks and delivery vans are brought there by ferry solely to unload heavy cargo, food supplies, and building materials from the ships. They can only drive back and forth for a few meters within that tiny harbor area. Once the goods hit the edge of the port, everything is immediately loaded onto the backs of donkeys to go up the hill.So while you will spot a vehicle or two sitting at the pier, the rest of the island is completely untouched by wheels. Hope this clears things up
